```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(deconflate)
```

Any input can be uncertain: a disease probability, an association row, an
impact row (including interactions), and, for event impacts, the overall
risk. `deconflate()` draws the uncertain inputs from their
distributions, adjusts each draw in the same way as the central estimate,
and reports intervals. Monte Carlo runs are part of `deconflate()`
(`n_draws`).

## Input distributions

`dist_*()` functions describe uncertain inputs. Draws are on the scale the
inputs were entered on (e.g. percent impacts, odds ratios, incidence rates).

```{r}
dist_pert(1.19, 3.30, 10.71)        # min, mode, max
dist_lognormal_ci(2.7, 1.5, 4.9)    # odds ratio and 95% CI
dist_normal(2.63, 1.44, lower = 0)  # truncated at zero
```

The others are `dist_fixed()`, `dist_lognormal()`, `dist_beta()`,
`dist_pert_mean()`, `dist_uniform()` and `dist_mixture()` (e.g. two pooled
sources of evidence); see `?distributions`.

## Where distributions are given

In input tables, an uncertain value gets its distribution in its own row,
in the columns `dist` and `p1`-`p4`, and `cm_read_inputs()` keeps it in the
model (see `vignette("own-data")`). In R, give them to `cm_model()` as
`distributions`, a named list whose names are keys: `prob:<disease>`,
`associations:<row>` and `impacts:<row>` (rows numbered from 1 in each
table). Shorter keys name the usual rows: `assoc:<d1>:<d2>` (a pair's crude
row), `impact:<disease>` (a disease's row), `inter:<d1>:<d2>` (an
interaction adjusted for all) and `three:<d1>:<d2>:<d3>` (an `OR_ratio`
row). Inputs without a distribution keep their point value in every draw.

```{r}
m <- example_supplement()
mu <- cm_model(m, m$impacts, distributions = list(
  "prob:d1" = dist_beta(20, 180),
  "assoc:d1:d2" = dist_lognormal_ci(2, 1.4, 2.9),
  "impact:d1" = dist_normal(2.5, 0.5),
  "impact:d2" = dist_normal(5, 1),
  "impact:d3" = dist_pert(5, 7.5, 9)
))
mu
```

## Draws and intervals

When any input has a distribution, `deconflate()` runs `n_draws` draws
(1000 by default; here 200 to keep this vignette fast). Each draw is a
complete set of inputs, so the uncertainty of probabilities, associations
and impacts is propagated jointly:

```{r}
r <- deconflate(mu, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
r
```

The central estimate (`adjusted`) always uses the point values; the draws
give the 95% intervals (`lower`, `upper`: the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles over
the accepted draws). The intervals are added to the adjusted impacts, the
contributions and the adjusted total:

```{r}
r$contributions
r$totals
```

`$draws` holds the details: `summary` (mean, standard deviation, Monte
Carlo standard error `mcse`, interval, median and a stability check for
every quantity), the accepted draws (`values`, and the drawn inputs in
`params`), the rejections and the seed:

```{r}
r$draws$summary
```

The stability check is `ok`, `imprecise` (the Monte Carlo standard error is
more than 5% of the mean: use more draws, or Latin hypercube sampling),
`heavy_tail` (the most extreme 1% of draws contribute more than 60% of the
variance) or `insufficient_info` (the precision cannot be assessed, e.g.
because the mean is zero; `mcse` still gives the absolute error). A note
lists the quantities that are not `ok`.

Without any distribution, no draws are run, whatever `n_draws`, and a note
says so; `n_draws = 0` skips the draws (and the note) for a model that has
distributions:

```{r}
deconflate(example_supplement())$notes
```

### Seed

Draws are reproducible with `seed`. Without it, a seed is chosen and stored
in the result, so a run can always be repeated:

```{r}
r_again <- deconflate(mu, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
identical(r$adjusted, r_again$adjusted)
r_unseeded <- deconflate(mu, n_draws = 200)
r_unseeded$draws$seed
```

### Rejected draws

Some draws are impossible: a probability outside (0, 1), a non-positive
odds ratio, or associations that no population can have together. Such
draws are rejected and not replaced, so the intervals describe the
accepted draws only. The number rejected is printed with the result, each
rejection is listed by type with its reason in `$draws$rejections`, and a
note appears when more than 10% are rejected. Here a prevalence is given a
normal distribution that reaches below zero:

```{r}
m_rej <- cm_model(m, m$impacts, distributions = list("prob:d1" = dist_normal(0.05, 0.05)))
r_rej <- deconflate(m_rej, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
r_rej
head(r_rej$draws$rejections, 3)
```

Draws can also be rejected because the values cannot hold together, even
when each is valid alone. Three diseases with strong odds ratios are
feasible at their point values, but not when one of them is much weaker
(`warn = FALSE` hides a warning that these made-up impacts change sign):

```{r}
strong <- cm_model(
  cm_diseases(c("a", "b", "c"), c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)),
  cm_impacts(c("a", "b", "c"), c(4, 5, 6)),
  associations = cm_associations(c("a", "a", "b"), c("b", "c", "c"), c(20, 20, 20)),
  distributions = list("assoc:a:b" = dist_lognormal_ci(20, 1, 400))
)
r_strong <- deconflate(strong, n_draws = 200, seed = 1, warn = FALSE)
r_strong$draws$n_rejected
table(r_strong$draws$rejections$type)
r_strong$draws$rejections$reason[1]
```

Report the rejection share: conditioning on acceptance changes the
effective input distribution. A high share means the input distributions
often combine values that contradict each other; narrower or correlated
evidence may be needed.

### Latin hypercube sampling

`sampling = "lhs"` stratifies each input's distribution, which usually
reduces the Monte Carlo error of means. Latin hypercube draws are not
independent, so they are split into `lhs_replicates` independent blocks (10
by default), and the Monte Carlo standard error is estimated from the
spread of the block means. Compare `mcse` with the random draws above:

```{r}
r_lhs <- deconflate(mu, n_draws = 200, seed = 1, sampling = "lhs")
r_lhs
data.frame(quantity = r$draws$summary$quantity,
           mcse_random = r$draws$summary$mcse,
           mcse_lhs = r_lhs$draws$summary$mcse)
```

## Several rows for one item

When several association rows are pooled (see `vignette("interactions")`),
each draw draws every row from its own distribution and pools the drawn
values with the weights of the central estimate. With random effects
(the default), the draw also adds the between-study spread: a standard
normal draw times tau, on the log scale, listed among the drawn inputs as
`between:associations:<rows>`. Impact rows that over-determine the impacts are fitted in
each draw by weighted least squares, with the weights of the central
estimate. Here two studies of the d1:d2 odds ratio disagree (I^2 above
90%):

```{r}
a2 <- cm_associations(c("d1", "d1", "d1", "d2"), c("d2", "d2", "d3", "d3"), c(1.8, 4, 1, 3))
m2 <- cm_model(m$diseases, m$impacts, associations = a2,
               distributions = list("associations:1" = dist_lognormal_ci(1.8, 1.3, 2.5),
                                    "associations:2" = dist_lognormal_ci(4, 3.4, 4.7)))
r2 <- deconflate(m2, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
r2$heterogeneity
grep("between", names(r2$draws$specs), value = TRUE)
r2_fixed <- deconflate(m2, n_draws = 200, seed = 1, pool = "fixed")
rbind(random = unlist(r2$totals[c("adjusted_total", "adjusted_total_lower", "adjusted_total_upper")]),
      fixed = unlist(r2_fixed$totals[c("adjusted_total", "adjusted_total_lower", "adjusted_total_upper")]))
```

The fixed-effect interval is narrower: it treats the two studies as
estimates of one value, which their disagreement contradicts.

## Event impacts: the overall risk

For event impacts (`vignette("event-impacts")`), the impacts can have
distributions like any other input, and `overall_risk` can be a
distribution too. The central estimate uses the mean of that distribution:

```{r}
cull <- cm_model(m, cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(1.5, 2.0, 1.2),
                               measure = c("HR", "HR", "RR"), label = "culling"))
e <- deconflate(cull, event_model = TRUE, overall_risk = dist_beta(250, 750),
                n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
e
e$attributable$summary
```

Here only the overall risk is uncertain. The attributable risk and its
allocation to diseases vary with it, while the adjusted hazard ratios
hardly change: raw hazard ratios do not depend on the overall risk, and
only the risk ratio of d3 does.

## Gaps and values over the draws

The package reports impacts in their own units. A gap or a value per draw
is computed in base R from the accepted draws in `$draws$values` (one row
per draw, one column per quantity). Here the impacts are percent losses of
an observed level of 10,000 units, and the value of a unit is drawn per
draw:

```{r}
total <- r$draws$values[, "total"]
gap <- 10000 / (1 - total / 100) - 10000
set.seed(5)
value <- gap * runif(length(gap), 0.25, 0.35)
sapply(list(gap = gap, value = value),
       function(x) c(mean = mean(x), quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975))))
```

The central gap uses the central total:

```{r}
10000 / (1 - r$totals$adjusted_total / 100) - 10000
```

## Ranks over the draws

With draws, `$ranks` gives the share of draws in which each disease ranks
first, second and so on by its contribution, and its mean rank.
`summary()` prints it with the totals and contributions:

```{r}
summary(r)
```

## Sensitivity

The draws give the joint uncertainty of the results. `cm_sensitivity()`
shows where it comes from, and what inputs that were not entered could
do. It reruns the adjustment with one input at a time at a low and a high
value, everything else at its central value (point estimates, adjusted as
`deconflate()` adjusts them; as in Rasmussen et al. 2024, Fig. 7):

* entered inputs move one SD down and up when they have a distribution,
  otherwise by `change` (20% by default);
* inputs that were not entered are set over a default range: an odds ratio
  from 0.5 to 3 for each pair that no row mentions, an interaction for each
  pair without a combination row, and, with `three_way`, `OR_ratio` rows
  (see `?cm_sensitivity`).

Given a result with draws, the column `share` adds each uncertain input's
share of the variance of the total over the draws (from a linear fit of
the total on the drawn inputs; `$r_squared` says how well it fits):

```{r}
s <- cm_sensitivity(r)
s
s$variance
```

The prevalence of d3 has a large swing, but it has no distribution, so it
adds nothing to the intervals. Of the uncertain inputs, the impact of d3
explains about half of the variance. `plot(s)` draws the swings as a
tornado plot.

The pairs that no row mentions (here d1 and d3) are varied too, so the
table shows which missing estimates would matter, next to the uncertainty
of those entered. `ranges` sets other ranges, and a model can be given
instead of a result:

```{r}
m_pairs <- cm_model(
  cm_diseases(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20)),
  cm_impacts(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), c(2.5, 5, 7.5)),
  associations = cm_associations(c("d1", "d2"), c("d2", "d3"), c(2, 3))
)
cm_sensitivity(m_pairs, ranges = data.frame(input = "pair:d1:d3", low = 0.5, high = 5))
```

Here an unknown odds ratio of d1 and d3 between 0.5 and 5 would change the
aggregate more than any entered association.

Runs that cannot be adjusted are reported, with the reason in column
`failed`, not skipped. In the strong model above, an odds ratio of 1
between a and c (or b and c) cannot hold with the other two at 20:

```{r}
keys <- c("associations:2", "associations:3")
cm_sensitivity(deconflate(strong, n_draws = 0, warn = FALSE), keys = keys,
               ranges = data.frame(input = keys, low = 1, high = 40))
```

`cm_sensitivity()` also works on a model without any association rows:
the diseases are then unrelated, and the table shows which pairs would
matter if they were associated. `cm_threshold()` finds the value of one
input at which a result changes (see `vignette("thresholds-and-scaling")`),
and `vignette("interactions")` covers interactions and three-way
associations.
